How to read a METAR

A METAR is a routine airport weather observation, usually issued every hour. The groups always come in the same order:

  1. Station and time: the ICAO code, then day and time in UTC (Zulu). 131953Z is the 13th at 19:53 UTC.
  2. Wind: direction in degrees true, speed in knots, and gusts after a G. 30018G27KT is from 300° at 18 knots, gusting 27.
  3. Visibility: statute miles in the US (10SM), metres elsewhere (9999 means 10 km or more).
  4. Weather: - light, + heavy, then codes like RA rain, SN snow, BR mist, FG fog, TS thunderstorm.
  5. Clouds: FEW, SCT, BKN or OVC plus the base in hundreds of feet. BKN015 is broken cloud at 1,500 ft above ground.
  6. Temperature and dew point in °C. An M means minus.
  7. Altimeter: A3002 is 30.02 inHg; Q1013 is 1013 hPa.
  8. Remarks after RMK, such as AO2 (automated station with a precipitation sensor) or SLP (sea-level pressure).

Flight categories

CategoryCeilingVisibility
VFRabove 3,000 ftmore than 5 SM
MVFR1,000–3,000 ft3–5 SM
IFR500 to below 1,000 ft1 to below 3 SM
LIFRbelow 500 ftbelow 1 SM

The ceiling is the lowest broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC) layer, or vertical visibility (VV). The worse of ceiling and visibility sets the category. These are the categories used by the Aviation Weather Center.

Live reports come from aviationweather.gov (NOAA). This decoder is a study aid, not an official weather briefing. Always get an official briefing before you fly.
